title: Git Fundamentals
summary: Git is the version control system used by virtually every software project. Understanding the three trees, how commits are built, and how branching works gives you the mental model to get out of any situation git gets you into.

sections.title: The three trees: working directory, index, and HEAD
sections.body:
## How Git actually stores your work

Most version control systems track changes as *diffs* — records of what lines changed between versions. Git takes a fundamentally different approach: it stores **snapshots**. Every commit is a complete picture of your entire repository at that moment in time, not a diff from the previous state. Diffs are computed on the fly when you ask for them. This design choice is why Git is so fast at switching branches and inspecting history.

**The object model:** Git is, at its core, a **content-addressed key-value store**. Every piece of data — every file, every directory listing, every commit — is stored as an object in `.git/objects/`. Each object is identified by the SHA-1 hash of its content. There are four object types:

- **blob** — the contents of a single file (no filename, just data)
- **tree** — a directory listing: names, permissions, and pointers to blobs and other trees
- **commit** — a pointer to a tree (the root directory snapshot), plus metadata: author, timestamp, message, and a pointer to the parent commit(s)
- **tag** — a named pointer to a specific commit

**Why content addressing matters:** If two files have identical content, they share a single blob object — Git never stores the same data twice. If you rename a file without changing it, Git knows it's the same blob. If you change one line in a file, only the new blob is stored; unchanged parts of the repository are referenced by the same objects as before. This makes Git both space-efficient and cryptographically tamper-evident — you can't change a commit without changing its hash and invalidating every subsequent commit that references it.

**The three trees:** Git manages three distinct snapshots of your codebase simultaneously:

1. **Working directory** — the files you actually see and edit on disk. Git doesn't manage this directly; it's just your filesystem.
2. **Index (staging area)** — a proposed next commit. `git add` copies content from the working directory into the index. The index is stored in `.git/index`.
3. **HEAD** — a pointer to the current commit (the last commit on the current branch). When you run `git commit`, Git takes the index snapshot, wraps it in a commit object, and moves HEAD forward.

**The mental model for daily work:** Think of it as a two-step process. First you *stage* changes (curate exactly what the next commit will contain). Then you *commit* (permanently record that snapshot). This separation lets you commit only part of your changes, stage changes from multiple files into a single logical commit, or split a big change into multiple focused commits — all without affecting the files you're editing.

Git manages three distinct areas. Confusing them is the root cause of most git mistakes.

```
┌─────────────────────────┐
│   Working Directory     │  ← files you see and edit
│   (untracked changes)   │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ git add
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│   Index (Staging Area)  │  ← changes staged for next commit
│   .git/index            │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │ git commit
             ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│   Repository (HEAD)     │  ← permanent history of commits
│   .git/objects/         │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

```bash norun
# See what's in each area
git status          # working dir vs index vs HEAD
git diff            # working dir vs index (what's NOT staged)
git diff --staged   # index vs HEAD (what WILL be committed)
git diff HEAD       # working dir vs HEAD (everything changed)
git log --oneline   # history of commits at HEAD

# The git object model — everything is content-addressed SHA1
git cat-file -t HEAD       # type of HEAD object (commit)
git cat-file -p HEAD       # contents of the HEAD commit
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree} # the tree (directory snapshot) it points to

# This is why git is reliable: every commit ID is a hash of its content.
# Changing any file changes the commit hash, making history tamper-evident.
```

**The key insight:** `git add` moves changes to the index. `git commit` moves the index to a new commit object. The working directory is just your local copy — it doesn't affect history until you `git add`.

sections.title: Core commands: init, add, commit, log, diff
sections.body:
## The commands you'll use every day

Git's command surface is large, but 80% of daily work uses fewer than a dozen commands. Understanding *why* each command works the way it does — not just the syntax — is what allows you to recover from mistakes and handle edge cases confidently.

**`git add` and the staging philosophy:** Unlike many VCS tools that commit all changes automatically, Git requires you to explicitly choose what goes into each commit. This is a feature, not a limitation. It lets you commit one logical change at a time even if you've been editing several unrelated things. `git add -p` (patch mode) is especially powerful: it shows you each changed *hunk* individually and asks whether to stage it, letting you split a file's changes across multiple commits.

**Commit messages and why they matter:** A good commit message is a letter to the future engineer (often yourself) who will be debugging this code six months from now. The convention in most projects is: a short imperative subject line (under 72 characters), a blank line, then a more detailed body explaining *why* the change was made, not *what* changed (the diff already shows that). Formats like **Conventional Commits** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`) add machine-readable structure that CI systems and changelog generators can parse.

**`git log` as a debugging tool:** The commit history is documentation. `git log --oneline --graph --all` gives you a topological view of all branches. `git log -- path/to/file` shows every commit that touched a specific file — essential for tracking down when a bug was introduced. `git bisect` (binary search through history) can automatically find the exact commit that introduced a regression.

**`git diff` — the three comparisons:** This trips up many beginners. `git diff` compares the working directory to the index (shows unstaged changes). `git diff --staged` compares the index to HEAD (shows what will be in the next commit). `git diff HEAD` compares the working directory to HEAD (shows everything changed since the last commit). Understanding which comparison you want is fundamental to understanding your repository's current state.

**Undoing mistakes:** Git's undo primitives map to the three trees. `git restore <file>` discards working directory changes (unstages nothing). `git restore --staged <file>` moves changes back from the index to the working directory (unstages them without losing the edits). `git reset HEAD~1` moves the HEAD pointer back one commit, putting all those changes back into the working directory. `git revert <hash>` creates a *new* commit that undoes a previous one — the safe way to undo history that's already been shared.

**.gitignore and secrets hygiene:** One of the most important Git practices in DevOps is making sure secrets never enter the repository. Once a secret is committed and pushed, it must be considered compromised — it will exist in git history even after deletion. `.gitignore` prevents accidental staging of sensitive files, but it only works for *untracked* files. If you've already staged a file, `.gitignore` won't help. Pre-commit hooks that scan for patterns like API keys and passwords are an essential safety net.

```bash norun
# ── Initialize a repo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
git init my-project
cd my-project

# Configure identity (required for commits)
git config --global user.name  "Esteban Moreno"
git config --global user.email "esteban@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# ── Staging and committing ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
git add file.txt          # stage a specific file
git add .                 # stage all changes
git add -p                # interactively choose hunks to stage (powerful)
git reset HEAD file.txt   # unstage a file (keep working dir changes)
git checkout -- file.txt  # discard working dir changes (destructive!)

git commit -m "feat: add deployment config for web-app"
git commit -am "fix: correct replica count"  # add + commit tracked files

# ── Viewing history ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
git log                           # full log
git log --oneline                 # compact
git log --oneline --graph --all   # graph view of all branches
git log --oneline -10             # last 10 commits
git log --author="Esteban"        # by author
git log -- path/to/file           # commits that changed a file
git show abc1234                  # show a specific commit

# ── Undoing things ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Amend last commit (only if not pushed!)
git commit --amend -m "corrected message"

# Revert a commit (creates a new commit that undoes it — safe for shared history)
git revert abc1234

# Reset HEAD (careful with --hard)
git reset HEAD~1           # undo last commit, keep changes staged
git reset HEAD~1 --soft    # same, keep changes staged
git reset HEAD~1 --hard    # undo last commit AND discard changes (destructive)

# ── .gitignore ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Prevent committing secrets, build artifacts, local config
cat > .gitignore << 'EOF'
# Python
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/

# Secrets
.env
*.key
*.pem
credentials.json

# Build artifacts
dist/
build/
*.tar.gz

# Editor
.vscode/
.idea/
EOF

# See what's ignored
git check-ignore -v filename
```

sections.title: Branching and merging
sections.body:
## Branching: Git's most powerful feature

A **branch** in Git is simply a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit. That's all it is — a 41-byte file in `.git/refs/heads/` containing a commit hash. Creating a branch doesn't copy files or create new objects; it just creates a new pointer. This is why Git branching is instantaneous and nearly free, unlike older version control systems (like SVN) where branching was expensive and discouraged.

**How branches work internally:** When you make a new commit on a branch, Git creates the commit object and moves the branch pointer forward to point to it. A special pointer called **HEAD** tells Git which branch you're currently on. When you switch branches with `git switch`, Git updates HEAD to point to the new branch and updates the working directory to match that branch's latest commit.

**Why feature branches matter:** The **trunk-based development** and **GitHub Flow** models — both common in DevOps teams — both rely on short-lived feature branches. The idea is: `main` (or `master`) always represents a deployable state. Every change, no matter how small, starts as a branch, goes through a pull request review, passes CI checks, and then merges back. This prevents broken code from reaching `main` and gives you a review checkpoint for every change.

**Merging strategies:**

- **Fast-forward merge:** When your branch hasn't diverged from main (i.e., no one committed to main while you were working), Git can simply move the main pointer forward. No merge commit is created. History stays linear. Clean, but you lose the record that a feature branch existed.
- **Three-way merge:** When both branches have diverged, Git finds the common ancestor, applies both sets of changes, and creates a **merge commit** with two parents. This preserves the full history of parallel work but adds visual complexity.
- **Squash merge:** All commits from the feature branch are combined into one commit on main. Great for keeping main's history clean, but you lose the incremental commit history from the branch.

**Rebase vs. merge:** `git rebase` replays your branch's commits on top of the target branch, rewriting each commit's hash. The result is a linear history with no merge commits — as if you had written your changes after main's latest commit. This looks cleaner but has a crucial rule: **never rebase commits you've already pushed to a shared branch**. Rewriting history changes commit hashes, which breaks everyone else who has those commits in their local copy.

**Merge conflicts:** Conflicts happen when two branches modify the same lines of the same file. Git marks the conflict in the file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers and stops the merge. You resolve it by editing the file to the correct final state, `git add`-ing it, and completing the merge. Conflicts are not errors — they're Git telling you it needs a human decision about how to combine two sets of changes.

**The stash — a temporary shelf:** `git stash` saves your current working directory and index changes to a stack, then restores HEAD. It's useful when you need to quickly switch contexts (e.g., fix an urgent bug on main) without committing half-finished work. Think of it as a clipboard for uncommitted changes.

Branches are cheap, disposable pointers to commits. They're how you isolate work and collaborate.

```bash norun
# ── Create and switch branches ────────────────────────────────────────────
git branch feature/add-nginx       # create branch
git switch feature/add-nginx       # switch to it (modern syntax)
git switch -c feature/add-nginx    # create AND switch in one step
git checkout -b feature/add-nginx  # old syntax (same result)

git branch                         # list local branches
git branch -a                      # include remote branches
git branch -d feature/done         # delete merged branch
git branch -D feature/abandoned    # force delete (unmerged)

# ── Merging ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
git switch main
git merge feature/add-nginx        # merge feature into main

# Types of merge:
# - Fast-forward: no divergence, pointer just moves forward (no merge commit)
# - 3-way merge: diverged history, creates a merge commit

git merge --no-ff feature/add-nginx  # force merge commit even if fast-forward possible
git merge --squash feature/add-nginx # squash all commits into one (then commit manually)

# ── Merge conflicts ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# When the same lines changed in both branches:
# Git marks the file with conflict markers:

# <<<<<<< HEAD
# replicas: 2
# =======
# replicas: 5
# >>>>>>> feature/scale-up

# Resolution process:
# 1. Edit the file to the correct state
# 2. git add the resolved file
# 3. git commit (or git merge --continue)

# Abort a merge in progress:
git merge --abort

# ── Rebase ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch
# Result: cleaner linear history, no merge commits

git switch feature/my-work
git rebase main              # replay feature commits on top of current main

# Interactive rebase — rewrite history (squash, reorder, edit commits)
git rebase -i HEAD~3         # interactive rebase of last 3 commits
# In the editor: pick/squash/reword/drop/edit each commit

# Golden rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch
# Rebase rewrites commit hashes — it breaks everyone else's history

# ── Stash — save work without committing ─────────────────────────────────
git stash                    # save working dir changes temporarily
git stash push -m "wip: nginx config"  # with a name
git stash list               # see all stashes
git stash pop                # restore last stash and remove it
git stash apply stash@{1}    # restore specific stash, keep it in list
git stash drop stash@{0}     # delete a stash
```

sections.title: Remote repositories: clone, fetch, pull, push
sections.body:
A remote is a copy of the repository hosted elsewhere (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket).

```bash norun
# ── Clone ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git       # HTTPS
git clone git@github.com:org/repo.git           # SSH (uses SSH key)
git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git mydir # clone into specific dir

# ── Remote management ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
git remote -v                # list remotes with URLs
git remote add origin https://github.com/org/repo.git  # add a remote
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:org/repo.git  # change URL
git remote remove upstream   # remove a remote

# ── Fetch, pull, push ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
git fetch origin             # download remote changes WITHOUT merging
git fetch --all              # fetch from all remotes

git pull origin main         # fetch + merge (or rebase with --rebase)
git pull --rebase origin main  # fetch + rebase (cleaner history)

git push origin main         # push local main to remote
git push -u origin feature/my-branch  # push new branch and set upstream
git push origin --delete feature/done # delete remote branch
git push --force-with-lease  # force push (safer: fails if remote changed)

# ── Tracking branches ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# After git push -u, git knows the upstream and you can just:
git pull
git push

# See tracking relationships
git branch -vv

# ── Tags ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
git tag v1.2.3               # lightweight tag
git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "release 1.2.3"  # annotated tag (recommended)
git push origin v1.2.3       # push specific tag
git push origin --tags       # push all tags

# ── SSH key setup for GitHub/GitLab ─────────────────────────────────────
sssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "esteban@example.com"
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub  # copy this to GitHub/GitLab SSH keys
# Test:
ssh -T git@github.com
```

sections.title: Exercise: practice branching and resolving conflicts
sections.body:
Simulate a real development workflow with feature branches and a merge conflict.

```bash
cd /workspace

# Clean up from previous runs
rm -rf gitlab-helper

# 1. Initialize a repo and make an initial commit
git config --global user.name 'DevOps Student'
git config --global user.email 'student@example.com'
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git init gitlab-helper
cd gitlab-helper
cat > README.md << 'EOF'
# GitLab Helper
A CLI tool for GitLab CI management.
EOF
git add README.md
git commit -m "chore: initial commit"

# 2. Create a feature branch and add a file
git switch -c feature/add-config
cat > config.yaml << 'EOF'
api_url: https://gitlab.example.com
timeout: 30
EOF
git add config.yaml
git commit -m "feat: add config file"

# 3. Simulate a concurrent change on main
git switch main
cat > config.yaml << 'EOF'
api_url: https://gitlab.corp.com
debug: false
EOF
git add config.yaml
git commit -m "feat: add config with corp URL"

# 4. Now try to merge the feature branch — conflict!
git merge feature/add-config
# git will report a conflict in config.yaml

# 5. Resolve the conflict manually:
cat config.yaml  # see the conflict markers
# Edit the file to keep both timeout and debug, use corp URL:
cat > config.yaml << 'EOF'
api_url: https://gitlab.corp.com
timeout: 30
debug: false
EOF
git add config.yaml
git commit -m "merge: resolve config conflict"

# 6. View the history
git log --oneline --graph --all

# 7. Squash the last 2 commits into one (non-interactive approach)
# 'git rebase -i HEAD~2' opens an editor — use soft reset instead:
git reset --soft HEAD~2
git commit -m "feat: add complete config (squashed)"
git log --oneline
```
